## Verification

**Tree and cut times.** The finger at spine vertex $(i,0)$ is the path $(i,1),\dots,(i,i)$, and $\lambda<1$ biases the walk toward each leaf. Since fingers are finite and the future of a cut time is infinite, cut times occur only when the walk crosses a spine edge $e_i=\{(i,0),(i+1,0)\}$ for the only time. Such a crossing time is the first hitting time of $(i+1,0)$.

**Crossing probability.** Finger excursions always return to their base, so the spine projection is a biased walk with $p_{\text{right}}=\frac{1}{1+\lambda}$ and $p_{\text{left}}=\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}$. From $(i+1,0)$, the probability of ever hitting $(i,0)$ is $q/p=\lambda$. So $\mathbb{P}(e_i \text{ crossed exactly once})=1-\lambda$. This is exact, and the proposed solution gets it right.

**Density of cut edges.** The up-crossing counts $U_i$ of the spine edges form a Markov chain (Ray–Knight type). Assuming it is positive recurrent with stationary marginal $\mathrm{Geom}(1-\lambda)$, the ergodic theorem gives $C_n/n\to 1-\lambda$ a.s. I did not verify positive recurrence in detail, but the marginal computation is consistent with it.

**Time to reach level $n$.** Once the walk enters a finger of length $i$ and is pushed to the leaf, returning to the base takes expected time of order $\lambda^{-i}$. This follows from the reversible measure $\pi(k)\propto\lambda^{-k}$ on the finger. Each finger is entered with probability bounded below, so $\log T_{(n,0)}/n\to\log(1/\lambda)$ a.s. The upper and lower bounds sketched in the proposed solution are plausible. I did not check every constant, but only the exponential rate matters here.

**Combining.** $M(N)=C_{n(N)-1}$ with $n(N)\sim \frac{\log N}{\log(1/\lambda)}$ a.s. Therefore
$$
\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{M(N)}{\log N}=\frac{1-\lambda}{\log(1/\lambda)}\quad\text{a.s.}
$$

**Sanity checks.** As $\lambda\to1^-$, the limit tends to $1$, which is consistent with the walk becoming a simple biased walk where almost every spine edge is a cut edge and time is roughly linear in level. As $\lambda\to0^+$, the limit tends to $0$, consistent with deep traps.

**Formatting.** The final answer as written, "(1 - lambda)/log(1/lambda, E)", contains a stray "E". I read it as $\frac{1-\lambda}{\log(1/\lambda)}$ with the natural logarithm, which matches the boxed result in the proposed solution.

The argument is sound at the level of exponential rates, and the constant $\frac{1-\lambda}{\log(1/\lambda)}$ follows from the two ingredients above.
